ref: Innocentius III, Regest. lib. XVI, bull XXVIII (Migne numbering) 'Universis Christi fidelibus per Maguntinensem provinciam constitutis', Migne PL 216, col. 818
quote_orig: sed ex tunc quidam perditionis filius, Machometus pseudopropheta, surrexit, qui per seculares illecebras et voluptates carnales multos a veritate seduxit; cujus perfidia etsi usque ad hac tempora invaluerit, confidimus tamen in Domino, qui jam fecit nobiscum signum in bonum, quod finis hujus bestie appropinquat
own_translation_en: But then a certain son of perdition, Muhammad the false prophet, arose, who seduced many from the truth through worldly enticements and carnal pleasures; although his perfidy has grown strong even until these times, we trust in the Lord, who has already shown us a sign for good, that the end of this beast is drawing near.
licence_note: Migne PL 216 (public domain, Migne d. 1875); archive.org OCR text layer, read by me. No public-domain English translation found; own_translation_en is the team's literal translation.
keys: per seculares illecebras et voluptates carnales multos a veritate seduxit
what_it_says: Innocent calls Muhammad a 'son of perdition' and 'false prophet' who arose and drew many from the truth by worldly allurements and carnal pleasures. He presents the Muslim power as a beast whose end is near.
context: The sentence sits inside the 1213 crusade bull that calls Christians to recover the Holy Land after the Saracens built a fortress on Mount Tabor and threaten Acre. Innocent frames Muhammad's rise as part of salvation history and the end-times, and it precedes the exhortation to take the cross and the indulgence.
limits: Very brief and classificatory: no argument about the Qur'an or Christ's doctrine. The sentence is embedded in the crusade appeal, so its point is partly rhetorical. Its wording is in Innocent's own voice. The 'sexcenta sexaginta sex' (666) apocalyptic calculation that follows it is an additional claim not quoted here. Famous status not verified: I found no scholarly citation of this sentence in the sources I read (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quia_maior quotes only 'pseudoprophet' and the incipit; it does not give this sentence).

ref: Pius II, Epistola ad Mahumetem, PDF page 51 of ita-bnc-in2-00000500-001 (folio not read)
quote_orig: in quo legitur verbum caro factum est. negat tuus legifer incarnationem verbi. nam cur inquit factus est deus homo & in ligno crucis passus, qui alio modo genus humanum redimere poterat. negat tua lex xpi necem & alium suo loco infectum existimat, nec deum incarnatum cognoscit, neque crucifixum aut mortuum. nos utrunque predicamus quia factus est deus homo & passus est, & propter salutem hominis hec facta esse testamur.
own_translation_en: ...in which it is read: 'the Word was made flesh.' Your lawgiver denies the incarnation of the Word. For why, he asks, was God made man and suffered on the wood of the cross, when he could have redeemed the human race otherwise? Your law denies the death of Christ and thinks another was put to death in his place; it does not recognise God made flesh, nor him crucified or dead. We preach both: that God was made man and suffered, and we testify that these things were done for the salvation of man.
what_it_says: Pius says the Qur'an's lawgiver denies the Incarnation and the crucifixion of Christ (a substitute is thought to have died in his place) and rejects the God-made-man of Christian faith.
context: Part of the Christological section of the letter, where Pius sets Christian doctrine (Trinity, Incarnation, Redemption) against the Qur'an as the letter's addressee would read it. It follows his exposition of the Trinity from scripture and is answered by 'nos utrunque praedicamus'.
limits: Pius paraphrases the Qur'an in his own voice; the 'inquit' is his reporting, not a verbatim Qur'anic quotation, and the Qur'an itself is not quoted. The line-break reading 'legi-tur' and 'incarnatio-nem' was joined per rule; 'xpi' is printed as the Christogram abbreviation and expanded here as 'Christi'. Famous status not verified.

ref: Pius II, Epistola ad Mahumetem, PDF page 69 of ita-bnc-in2-00000500-001 (folio not read)
quote_orig: recordaris tue legislatoris, qui asserit legem & prophetas a iudeis evangelium a christianis esse corruptum tantumque de veritate vel novi testamenti vel veteris remansisse quantum alcorano continet. exploratum id forsitan arbitraris & verum esse, atque idcirco testimoniis nostris non adhibes fidem, nec baptizari audes aut in xpm credere. utinam tam bonus fuisset tuus legifer quam callidus, tam verax quam versutus, tam iustus quam iniquus; tota est artificiosa & fraudulenta lex eius.
own_translation_en: Remember what your lawgiver asserts: that the Law and the Prophets were not corrupted by the Jews, but that the Gospel was corrupted by the Christians, and that only so much of the truth of the New or the Old Testament remains as is contained in the Qur'an. You think this is proven and true; so you give no faith to our testimonies, and you dare neither to be baptised nor to believe in Christ. [Would that / for] your lawgiver had been as good as he was crafty, as truthful as he was sly, as just as he was wicked; the whole of his law is artful and fraudulent.
keys: tota est artificiosa & fraudulenta lex eius
what_it_says: Pius charges the Qur'an with teaching that the Gospel was corrupted by Christians, so that little of Scripture remains true, and calls the lawgiver and his law crafty and fraudulent.
context: In the part of the letter that answers the Qur'an's charge of scriptural corruption; Pius wants Mehmed to refuse this claim and to accept the Gospel. He argues in the surrounding pages that the Scriptures were not corrupted.
limits: Harsh ad hominem flavour ('callidus', 'versutus', 'iniquus') aimed at Muhammad's law and lawgiver, in Pius's voice. The word 'utinam' is my reading of the line-break 'uti-' / 'nam' joined per rule; the sentence syntax is uncertain. The Qur'an is described, not quoted. Harshness 5 for the 'fraudulenta' verdict.

quote_orig: vita flumina lactis & mellis & vini promittit & cibaria delicata & uxores multas & concubinas & virginum coitus & angelorum in turpibus obsequiis ministeria & quidquid caro deposcit. bonus hic paradisus & asini potius quam hominis est. Tua lex ideo vitam appetendam hominis existimat, ut edat & bibat, sicut in hoc saeculo carneus fuit legifer tuus, ita & in futuro carnis studendum putavit.
own_translation_en: ...[the law] promises rivers of milk, honey and wine, delicate foods, many wives and concubines, intercourse with virgins and the service of angels in shameful duties, and whatever the flesh asks. This paradise is good, but better suited to an ass than to a man. Your law holds that the life of man is to be desired so that he may eat and drink; as your lawgiver was carnal in this age, so, it thinks, one ought to be careful in the next age about the flesh.
what_it_says: Pius says the Qur'an's paradise promises bodily pleasures (wine, food, wives, concubines, virgins) and that Muhammad's law and life were carnal, so that the afterlife is taught as bodily gratification.
context: In the section on what the Qur'an teaches about the next life and the moral life of man, set against Christian and classical moral teaching; Pius compares the Qur'an's promises with the philosophers' views of the highest good.
limits: Pius's own summary and irony; the Qur'an's paradise is described, not quoted. 'Bonus hic paradisus' is a sarcastic verdict. The paradise sentence is presented as the law's teaching, which is Pius's reading. 'Qui' form 'carneus' is his polemic. Famous status not verified.

quote_orig: Nec fefellit eum opinio in hac parte: placuit nova lex, & breui tempore ita coaluit ut in multis populis gentibus ac linguis reciperetur, cuius fundamenta in voluptate iacta fuerunt.
own_translation_en: His expectation in this respect was not wrong: the new law pleased, and in a short time it grew so strong that it was accepted among many peoples, nations and tongues; its foundations were laid in pleasure.
keys: cuius fundamenta in voluptate iacta fuerunt
in multis populis gentibus ac linguis reciperetur
what_it_says: Pius says that Muhammad's new law spread quickly among many peoples because its foundations were laid in pleasure; this is his explanation of how Islam spread.
context: Immediately before this sentence Pius says Muhammad found one way to propagate his law: by commanding what would please his hearers (a sentence I have not quoted, see limits). The paragraph then describes how the law took root among many peoples.
limits: Excluded from the quote: the preceding sentence ('ea praecipiens quae grata essent auditoribus et maxime plebibus que iumentis similes existunt') contains a demeaning generalisation about the common people, so I did not quote it (see excluded.json). The following sentences on forcing disputants with 'ferro' are not quoted (excluded.json). The point of this quote is historical/explanatory, not a call to violence.

quote_orig: Hunc secutus est Machumetes, qui salvandos per alcoranum malos angelos affirmat. Nos cum ysaya de omnibus damnatis sive hominibus sive angelis unam sententiam habemus, quod vermis eorum non morietur, et ignis eorum non extinguetur.
own_translation_en: Following him is Muhammad, who affirms that through the Qur'an the evil angels will be saved. We, with Isaiah, hold one judgement on all the damned, whether men or angels: their worm will not die and their fire will not be quenched.
keys: salvandos per alcoranum malos angelos affirmat
what_it_says: Pius says Muhammad, following an earlier heretical teacher (Origen, named in the preceding sentence), taught through the Qur'an that the evil angels would be saved, and that Christians hold the opposite (eternal punishment of the damned).
context: In the section on angels and the fate of the damned, where Pius sets out Christian angelology and eschatology against the Qur'an's teaching.
limits: The 'Origen' attribution is in the preceding sentence (not quoted) and is Pius's characterisation of universal salvation. The Qur'an is described, not quoted. The Isaiah reference is Pius's own citation. Harshness only 3: mostly doctrinal disagreement.

quote_orig: Dicit enim dominus deus: estote sancti, quia ego sanctus sum. Machumetes uxores inquit ducite & cocubinas quot placet. Nam ego quadraginta virorum in meis lumbis vires habeo & uxoribus atque ancillis permisceor plurimis.
own_translation_en: For the Lord God says: be holy, for I am holy. Muhammad says: take wives, he says, and concubines as many as you please. For I have the strength of forty men in my loins, and I mingle with many wives and maidservants.
keys: ego quadraginta virorum in meis lumbis vires habeo
what_it_says: Pius contrasts the Lord's call to holiness with Muhammad's permission of many wives and concubines, which he presents as Muhammad's own boast of sexual vigour.
context: In the section on the moral teaching of the Qur'an and Muhammad's claims to authority, where Pius argues that the Lord's commandments are not those of Muhammad.
limits: The second sentence is Pius's rhetorical voice, putting a boast in Muhammad's mouth; it is not a quotation of the Qur'an or the hadith and must not be presented as one. This is a personal/character attack on Muhammad, though its point is doctrinal (permitted polygamy). Use with that caveat; it may be judged an insult and held back by the orchestrator.

quote_orig: Quid est hoc nisi quod manifeste negat se miraculorum virtute carere, & ficta falsaque esse omnia signa demonstrat, que tue legis doctores in populis predicant?
own_translation_en: What is this but that he plainly denies that he lacks the power of miracles, and shows that all the signs which the doctors of your law proclaim among the peoples are fictitious and false?
keys: ficta falsaque esse omnia signa demonstrat
what_it_says: Pius argues that the Qur'an's own rejection of miracles (Muhammad claims he worked none) shows that the signs claimed by Islamic doctors are false.
context: Pius sets Christ's miracles (the Christian sign-argument, which he states in the lines before) against Muhammad's refusal to perform miracles; the question he asks points back to Muhammad's own sentence about the sword, which I did not quote.
limits: The sentence depends on a preceding claim that Muhammad's legitimacy rests on the sword (excluded, see excluded.json); this quote contains only the conclusion. Pius's reading of the Qur'an's stance on miracles is an interpretation, not a quotation. The word 'predicant' is printed 'predicant'; 'que' and 'falsaque' as printed.
